crawler.headline: AI crawler docs shifted from opaque to verifiable—IP ranges, UA strings, and opt-out mechanisms now standardized.
crawler.body: Over the past year, AI crawler documentation has undergone a structural shift toward operational transparency and tooling standardization. Major vendors (OpenAI, Amazon, Google, Anthropic, Perplexity) have published or clarified IP-range JSON endpoints, consolidated user-agent strings with explicit versioning, and formalized page-level opt-out mechanisms (notably Amazon's `noarchive` meta tag for model-training exclusion). Simultaneously, infrastructure platforms—chiefly Cloudflare—have introduced new crawler-verification and redirection features, including canonical-URL redirects for training-specific traffic and Radar-based visibility into crawler adoption patterns across the web. The emergence of the `llms.txt` convention and the expansion of publisher blocking toward archival infrastructure (`ia_archiverbot`) signal that both vendors and site operators are converging on machine-readable, standardized controls. UA-string stability has improved (GPTBot and OAI-SearchBot pinned at v1.3; CCBot clarified with full URL), though IP-range nomenclature shifts (Google's `googlebot.json` → `common-crawlers.json`) require tooling updates. The most significant operational change is the shift from "we do not publish IPs" (Anthropic's prior stance) to standardized JSON feeds, enabling IP-based verification and abuse reporting at scale.

ecosystem.headline: AI agent traffic and data scraping define regulatory and infrastructure battles in May
ecosystem.body: The last 30 days split cleanly between two fronts: infrastructure vendors racing to govern agentic AI traffic, and publishers fighting unauthorized content scraping. DataDome's May activity—five launches around Agent Trust, virtual waiting rooms, and intent-based triage—reflects a market surge in MCP (Model Context Protocol) traffic that Anthropic's connector expansion is now legitimizing at scale. Meanwhile, the News Media Alliance escalated legal pressure on scrapers, filing an amicus brief behind Amazon's suit against Perplexity and demanding Common Crawl enforce protections. The EU simplified its AI rulebook in early May with less friction than expected, creating space for the real friction points: how to distinguish legitimate agent-generated requests from scraping, and who controls access to content at the infrastructure layer. Waiting room and intent assessment are no longer edge cases—they're becoming table stakes for CDNs and platforms managing hybrid human-and-agent traffic.

agent.headline: Codex agents mature toward production deployment with security and infrastructure focus.
agent.body: Over the past month, OpenAI shifted the conversation around agent infrastructure from capability toward operational readiness. A security and compliance framework landed first, followed by Windows Sandbox isolation—both table-stakes for enterprise trust. Sea Limited's engineering deployment signals that early adopters are moving past proofs-of-concept into scaled, production use. Meanwhile, Parloa integration suggests the ecosystem is beginning to standardize around voice as a control surface for agents, widening the surface area beyond code-execution contexts. The coherence of these moves points to a hardening of the stack: agents are no longer experimental; they're being locked down for real work.
